query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of aluminum to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will improve its oxygen resistance by promoting the formation of a continuous, slow-growing protective alumina (Al2O3) scale without compromising its room- and high-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C with inadequate oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor aluminum addition (on the order of a few atomic percent, e.g. ~3–5 at.% Al) into the equiatomic alloy.
generation.conditions: Exposure to air at elevated temperatures (e.g., 800 °C for a duration of around 5 hours), with mechanical tests conducted at room temperature and at 1000 °C under strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, adherent, and thermodynamically stable alumina (α-Al2O3) scale that acts as a diffusion barrier for oxygen.
generation.mechanism: Selective oxidation of the added Al leads to the formation of an external protective Al2O3 layer that slows down further oxygen ingress. This modification is based on the well-known principle used in Nb-silicide-based alloys where an Al2O3 scale significantly improves oxidation resistance while preserving the alloy’s mechanical integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy will show reduced oxygen uptake and pesting under high-temperature exposure while retaining or minimally affecting the original ductility and yield strength. The formation of a protective alumina scale is expected to improve oxidation resistance relative to the untreated equiatomic alloy.
generation.baseline: The untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy, which lacks sufficient oxygen resistance, leading to pesting or accelerated oxidation during prolonged exposure at high temperatures.
generation.boundary: Intervention effectiveness is expected in air at around 800 °C for exposures on the order of 5 hours, with the alloy’s mechanical performance characterized at room temperature and 1000 °C. The aluminum content must be low enough (a few atomic percent) to avoid significant changes in phase stability and mechanical properties.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal aluminum concentration and its effect on microstructure and mechanical properties have some uncertainty. Excess aluminum might lead to unwanted phase changes or brittle behavior if not carefully optimized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr (control) and one set with a minor aluminum addition (e.g. 3–5 at.% Al). Expose both sets to air at 800 °C for 5 hours. After exposure, analyze the surface oxide scales using microscopy and X-ray diffraction to ascertain the continuity and composition of the scale. Additionally, perform room-temperature tensile tests and high-temperature (1000 °C) yield strength measurements at strain rates between 10^−4 and 10^−2 s^−1.
measurements: Thickness and continuity of the oxide scale via SEM/TEM and XRD analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminum-modified alloy does not form a continuous, protective alumina scale (or forms a poorly adherent or non-protective oxide) and/or exhibits a significant deterioration in room-temperature ductility or high-temperature yield strength compared to the control alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Nb-silicide based alloys (or Nb-silicide in situ composites) are new materials and strong candidates for structural applications in gas turbines at high temperatures where the surface temperature of the alloy should not exceed 1400 °C. Like the Ni-based superalloys that are used in the latest generation of gas turbines, the Nb-silicide based alloys will require a coating [,] but must have adequate oxidation resistance to “survive” in case of failure of the coating. Unlike the Ni-based superalloys that are not prone to pest oxidation, the Nb-silicide based alloys will also need to have good resistance to pest oxidation. Contamination of Nb-silicide based alloys by interstitial elements must be controlled. For high temperature applications, alloy developers aspire to discover alloys that can form compact protective self-healing oxide layer in which the diffusion of metal cations is inhibited (very slow). For Nb-silicide based alloys, coating system with alumina scale forming bond coat compatible with the substrate alloy is desirable []. An aim of this paper is to provide an insight into the design and selection of metallic materials for a coating system for Nb-silicide based alloys.

It is well known that specific alloying additions in Nb enhance its oxidation resistance [,,]. The latter increases with additions of Al, B, Cr, Ge, Hf, Mo, Si, Sn, and Ti in Nb-silicide-based alloys [,,,,,,,,,,], in which Si is the key addition needed to form silicide(s) and for oxidation. Silica can be stable to higher temperatures than alumina, has a lower activation energy for oxygen diffusion, and could be more effective than alumina at higher temperatures []. Amorphous silica has some fluidity to heal cracks in the scale. Alumina is crystalline with virtually no fluidity. The oxides of the alloying elements Al, Hf, and Ti are even more thermodynamically stable than silica. The latter has virtually no solubility with Nb2O5 in the solid state. B2O3 or GeO2 in silica gives (a) a glass with lower viscosity at low temperatures where the resulting higher fluidity can improve the self-healing of the scale, and (b) a higher coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) than pure silica []. The Nb-silicide-based alloys form complex oxide scales during oxidation [,,,,,,].
